relationships.name: Alexander Glasgow
relationships.evidence_grade: Possible father inferred from the combined Kirknewton households
relationships.basis: Prefer Alexander Glasgow-3118 as Andrew Glasgow-1546’s father at 58% subjective confidence, possible. The particular Alexander household is established at Kirknewton by the 1667 Margaret Smith marriage and the father-named Alexander and Agnes entries in 1673 and 1677. Andrew’s 1700 Christian Cook marriage and fatherhood of James in 1702 place his own adult household in the same parish, one generation later. The sustained parish setting and feasible household succession together favour this existing family. Andrew, Alexander and Agnes recur in the descendant branches, providing modest supporting context rather than an independent naming rule. This weighs a specific family against alternatives, rather than inferring fatherhood from surname and estimated ages alone. The 1685 birth is an unsourced estimate. Taken literally it makes Andrew about fifteen at the indexed 1700 marriage and seventeen at the 1702 christening. Those ages are possible, but they cannot independently support the pedigree. A birth earlier in the 1670s or early 1680s would also fit the adult events and Alexander’s family chronology; no replacement birth year is adopted. Alexander’s own circa-1650 birth is likewise an estimate. The argument rests chiefly on the recorded adult households, not on moving either birth date to fit.

claims.reason: Prefer Alexander Glasgow-3118 as Andrew Glasgow-1546’s father at 58% subjective confidence, possible. The particular Alexander household is established at Kirknewton by the 1667 Margaret Smith marriage and the father-named Alexander and Agnes entries in 1673 and 1677. Andrew’s 1700 Christian Cook marriage and fatherhood of James in 1702 place his own adult household in the same parish, one generation later. The sustained parish setting and feasible household succession together favour this existing family. Andrew, Alexander and Agnes recur in the descendant branches, providing modest supporting context rather than an independent naming rule. This weighs a specific family against alternatives, rather than inferring fatherhood from surname and estimated ages alone. The 1685 birth is an unsourced estimate. Taken literally it makes Andrew about fifteen at the indexed 1700 marriage and seventeen at the 1702 christening. Those ages are possible, but they cannot independently support the pedigree. A birth earlier in the 1670s or early 1680s would also fit the adult events and Alexander’s family chronology; no replacement birth year is adopted. Alexander’s own circa-1650 birth is likewise an estimate. The argument rests chiefly on the recorded adult households, not on moving either birth date to fit. No checked source names Andrew’s father. Another Kirknewton father remains possible: the older Andro account Glasgow-1319, or one of the local John or William households, cannot be excluded merely because no Andrew baptism has been identified. John Glasgow-1057 of Kilwinning/Stevenston remains a weaker comparison because his documented household is elsewhere. Common forenames and the inherited father attachment must not be counted as independent confirmation. The complete sibling and child sequences are not established. Margaret Smith is not assigned as Andrew’s mother.
